meta.title: Case study: a telco OSS data lake
hero.kicker: Case study · telco OSS data lake
hero.title: An OSS lake where people, services and AI agents share the data of every network device
hero.lead: A composite case: how one slow NOC screen led to the data in one place, shared by many teams and by AI agents.
hero.note: A composite scenario: a fictional operator and fictional cities, built from common telco OSS practice (medallion layering over 3GPP-style data). This PoC runs device traces only; performance counters (PM), alarms (FM) and complaints are sources in the figure. Names are invented; figures are measured in the PoC on generated data at reduced scale.
where.body: A telco runs two families of systems. BSS handles customers and money (subscriptions, rating, billing); OSS handles the network itself (equipment, faults, quality). This lake is on the OSS side.
arch.title: Architecture
arch.body: The whole lake of a typical telco OSS.
arch.aria: The lake in seven columns: sources, ingestion, bronze, silver, gold, serving, use
arch.contract.d: column names, descriptions and types are defined once in a contract file in Git, and every stage's schema and DDL is generated from it.
arch.control.d: topics, stream jobs, connectors, schemas and tables are declared, deployed and observed through an API instead of by hand. People and AI agents use the same API.
uc.title: Who uses it for what
uc.body: Many teams use the same data, each in its own way. The five large cards and the data-quality tile ran in the PoC; the other tiles describe common patterns that were not run here.
uc.noc.title: Where is it busy, where is it weak, where did something just break?
uc.noc.body: One screen with the grid cells that had the most users in the last hour (blue), the grid cells with the weakest signal (red), and the area whose signal dropped suddenly in the last minute (yellow). A grid cell is an H3 res-9 hexagon of about 0.1 km²: measurements are grouped by where they were taken, not by the serving radio cell.
uc.noc.how: How: only the answer the screen needs is precomputed every minute, so the screen opens at once. Grid outlines come from ClickHouse's H3 functions.
map.aria: {city}: {top} grid cells with most users, {weak} grid cells with weakest signal
map.tip.users: users rank {rnk} · {cell} · {users} users · avg RSRP {rsrp} dBm
map.tip.signal: weak-signal rank {rnk} · {cell} · avg RSRP {rsrp} dBm · {users} users
uc.dash.title: KPI trends that change every minute
uc.dash.body: A dashboard tool sends the same query every minute and draws the lines. Below is the weak-signal share per city over the last hour (weak signal: RSRP below −100 dBm, a tunable threshold); a spike means an area had an incident in that minute.
chart.aria: Weak-signal share per city over the last hour, three lines at one-minute steps
uc.dash.how: How: dashboard tools connect to ClickHouse directly. Even values that must be de-duplicated, such as user counts, are exact, by merging the states kept in the one-minute summary.
uc.analysis.title: Answering a question nobody prepared for
uc.analysis.body: Is weak signal (RSRP below −100 dBm) concentrated downtown or at the edge? A question nobody built a report for, asked on the spot in SQL.
uc.analysis.how: How: asked of the one-minute summary instead of the raw rows, joined with area data; that is what keeps it interactive (section 5 measures the difference).
uc.rest.title: Request/response: take it with one HTTP call
uc.rest.body: A consumer takes the data it needs with one HTTP request. Typically an API service in front of ClickHouse handles authentication and the catalogue, and lets the consumer pick the original format or the industry-standard model. Below: a request sent straight to ClickHouse's HTTP interface and the start of its response.
uc.rest.how: How: ClickHouse takes queries over HTTP and streams the result row by row as it is produced. No driver needed.
uc.alert.title: Subscription: tell me when something happens
uc.alert.body: When a grid cell's signal in the latest minute falls well below its own previous hour, that is an alert. Grid cells are folded per area into one line a person can read. Below: alerts raised in the PoC; the generator injects one sudden drop a minute so the pipeline has something to carry.
alert.line: {time} UTC · {district} (area {area}): {cells} grid cells, signal down {drop} dB
uc.alert.how: How: typically, when new data is ready an event goes out on a message queue saying "fetch now", and subscribers take it then. Results can also be pushed straight to a Kafka topic.
uc.bulk.title: Bulk export: take a lot at once
uc.bulk.body: When a large chunk is needed, for model training or loading another system, a whole period is exported at once.
uc.bulk.how: How: ClickHouse can write query results straight to object storage as files, or stream them over HTTP. It is a common next serving mode after request/response.
uc.pg.title: Managed Postgres: subscriptions, keys and business data in Postgres
uc.pg.body: A serving layer comes with small business data: subscriptions, API keys, how far each consumer has read (watermarks). It usually lives in Postgres. With ClickHouse's Managed Postgres that data and the lake sit in one cloud, and the pg_clickhouse extension lets plain Postgres SQL join the lake's alerts with owner teams and open tickets.
uc.pg.how: Basis: the same approach was verified in the pg_clickhouse lab of the clickhouse-managed-postgres-hols repository (2026-10-01).
uc.contract.title: Change the schema in one place and apply it at once
uc.contract.body: When each stage defines its own schema, names and meanings drift, and every change has to go through several teams. A common answer is one data-contract file in Git as the reference, from which CI generates the message schema, the lake table definition and the ClickHouse DDL.
uc.contract.how: How: ClickHouse takes the generated DDL as it is. Tables and MVs are plain SQL, so they are reviewed and deployed like code.
uc.quality.title: Checking incoming data at every stage
uc.quality.body: Measurements without a grid cell or a subscriber are dropped when data is refined; measurements without a signal value keep "missing", not 0. Row counts show what each stage dropped and kept.
uc.quality.how: How: the cleaning rules live in one place, the SQL of a materialized view, so rule and result are reviewed together. The original stays as received, so it can be rebuilt when a rule changes.
uc.obs.title: Observing the pipeline itself
uc.obs.body: With many collectors, topics, stream jobs and connectors, seeing where things slow down or fail becomes work of its own. Their logs, metrics and traces can go into the same ClickHouse.
uc.obs.how: How: ClickStack, the observability stack built on ClickHouse, takes OpenTelemetry data for search and dashboards.
uc.history.title: Old history and recent data together
uc.history.body: Long history stays in an open-table-format lake (Iceberg and others); recent data is used fast in ClickHouse. Reading both in one query makes reprocessing and long-term trends easier.
uc.history.how: How: ClickHouse can read Iceberg tables on object storage directly and join them with gold tables, without moving the lake.
uc.agent.title: Turning a question in plain language into SQL
uc.agent.body: An operator asks something like "which areas in City B lost signal in the last 30 minutes?"; the agent reads the catalogue and schema descriptions, writes SQL and asks the lake. The descriptions in the schema contract become the agent's context.
uc.agent.how: How: agents connect to ClickHouse over MCP or HTTP and query as a read-only user. Summary tables are what would keep answers fast when questions cannot be predicted; agent latency was not measured here.
uc.llmobs.title: Checking that agents answer correctly
uc.llmobs.body: Agents can be trusted only when their SQL, answers, cost and latency are recorded and evaluated.
uc.llmobs.how: How: Langfuse, which uses ClickHouse as its store, shows agent traces, evaluations and cost on the same platform.

eng.summary: For engineers: tables, transformations, SQL, measurements
eng.body: The four stages are the tables ue_trace_raw, ue_trace, cell_kpi_1m and cell_rank_now in database oss_lake. The first two links are materialized views, the last a refreshable materialized view that runs every minute. The use cases are the views in 04-usecases.sql. Measurements use LTE terms (RSRP, RSRQ, SINR; TS 36.214); each one's location is assumed to come from MDT location reports or positioning, mapped to an H3 grid cell.

pitfall.title: A pitfall found while building it.
pitfall.body: An aggregate state type has to match whether its source column is Nullable. A mismatched MV is refused at CREATE, but if the source column is made Nullable later with ALTER, every INSERT after it fails while the source keeps filling (reproduction in the README).
same.title: Every stage gives the same answer
same.body: Ask the same NOC question of each of the four stages and the same 20 rows come back (03-queries.sql checks it). Rows and the amount read shrink at every stage.

sit.title: Situation
sit.scr.aria: A NOC screen still loading its lists of busiest and weakest grid cells for the last hour
sit.body: An operator's OSS team runs a NOC screen showing, for the last hour, the grid cells with the most users and the grid cells with the weakest signal. Measurements from devices (UE: phones, IoT modules, vehicles, routers) were aggregated from the source every time, so the screen was slow.
sit.p1: In this scenario, re-reading the raw data for every screen could not meet interactive response times
sit.p2: Each stage defined its own schema; names and meanings drifted
sit.p3: Changing a pipeline or a schema took a long time
sit.p4: More unpredictable ad hoc questions, and queries from AI agents
trend.title: The industry trend: virtualizing the OSS data layer
trend.body: Instead of copying data into every system, operators are putting meaning and access control on top of one data layer, so people and AI agents use the same data. The layers below are the author's summary of public material; the layers are vendor-neutral, and the labels only show where this case places each product.
trend.l1.d: autonomous-operations agents, network digital twin, NOC · BI
trend.l2.d: standard Open APIs, MCP tool catalogue, policy · audit, a human gate before writes
trend.l3.d: ontology · knowledge graph, topology · inventory models, standard information model
trend.l4.d: curated, contracted data owned by each domain (gold)
trend.l5.d: history in an open-table lake, queried in place instead of copied
trend.l6.d: streaming from RAN · core · transport · probes, standardized network data collection
trend.l7.d: network functions, element management, OSS/BSS systems of record
arch.b.note: in real life one table per source and vendor software release
arch.o.limits: a user and limits per consumer
uc.alert.webhook: In production the same rows can be pushed straight to a webhook with the URL table engine.
built.region: Region summary: districts with the highest weak-signal share in the last hour
lesson.title: Lessons
lesson.a.title: Nullable costs mostly in query complexity
lesson.a.body: The same NOC query written on bronze and on silver. The marked NULL checks, conversions and hashing disappear on silver.
lesson.b.title: A uniq state is sized by distinct values per group, not by input type
lesson.b.body: Rather than hoping a type change shrinks it, choose the grain where user counts live (1 minute, 10 minutes).
lesson.b.types: One state: by input type and by distinct values
lesson.b.grain: All user-count states in the PoC: 1-minute and 10-minute grain
lesson.c.title: Build coarse rollups from fine ones
lesson.c.body: The 10-minute rollup is filled by an MV on the rows arriving in the 1-minute rollup, so raw data is aggregated once. A refreshable MV with APPEND would, by design, insert twice whenever its window is wider than its refresh interval.
lesson.c.ok: equal to a 10-minute aggregate computed straight from raw (a deliberate-mismatch control fires)
lesson.d.title: Time columns named for local time but typed UTC
lesson.d.body: Buckets and TTL shift by the UTC offset. Store instants with an explicit time zone.
lesson.d.fig: the same instant, only the label differs
lesson.e.title: Many consumers need their own users and limits
lesson.e.body: Dashboards, an AI agent over MCP, a data catalogue and Kafka Connect batches each load the system differently.
lesson.e.l1: read-only users with result-row and execution-time limits
lesson.e.l2: separate users for the agent and the catalogue
lesson.e.l3: larger batches or async inserts on the ingest side
lesson.measured: Lessons a–c measured 2026-10-18 in the PoC, ClickHouse 26.9.13.15; d–f are common practice, not measured here.

trend.pg: keeps the consumer side's usage patterns and work records (subscriptions, API keys, watermarks, tickets, agent actions and approvals) — transactional data — in ClickHouse's Managed Postgres, linked to the lake with pg_clickhouse.
cmp.imsi: vendor hash → 64-bit pseudonym (cityHash64). A pseudonym is still personal data; production hashes with a key kept outside the lake (HMAC).
demo.auto: Flowing by itself on ClickHouse Cloud, one minute at a time · now {t} (UTC)
demo.lead.auto: Every minute new measurements arrive in the lake on ClickHouse Cloud by themselves and pass through the four stages, so the numbers below change once a minute; data older than a day (gold: two days) is dropped. Click a stage to see a sample row and that stage's answer to the same NOC question.
hero.result: In the PoC the same 20 rows came back in {srv_ms} ms from the ready answer, instead of {raw_ms} ms re-aggregating {raw_rows} raw rows (measured {date}, generated data).
aud.exec: Executives: one shared data layer serves screens, analysts and AI agents; the expensive work is done once, not per viewer.
aud.sa: Sales and SAs: a pattern to propose: history stays in the lake, gold and the serving layer go into ClickHouse, start with one screen.
aud.eng: Engineers: medallion stages as materialized views, rollups built from rollups, a refreshed answer table; checks in 03–05.
sit.note: The PoC answers the first and the last of these. Schema drift and slow change are what the schema contract and the control-plane API in the architecture address; this PoC describes them but does not run them (see next steps).
lesson.f.title: A pseudonymous trace is still personal data
lesson.f.body: A grid cell, a timestamp and a stable hash per row are enough to rebuild one subscriber's movements. An unkeyed hash of an IMSI can be reversed by trying every number in the range.
lesson.f.l1: hash with a key held outside the lake (HMAC), rotated
lesson.f.l2: keep the row-level stage narrow and short-lived
lesson.f.l3: hide counts below a minimum in served results
cta.cost: Running this demo on ClickHouse Cloud adds about $3–5 a month in storage on an always-on service already in use (estimate, 2026-10-18).
next.title: Next steps
next.s1: Start with one screen: move one slow NOC or BI view onto a gold summary and a ready answer. Measure: screen response time.
next.s2: Share gold: let other teams and dashboards read the same summaries. Measure: number of consumers, ad hoc questions answered without a new pipeline.
next.s3: Open it to agents and external consumers: read-only users with limits, the schema contract in Git. Measure: schema-change lead time.
next.risks: Plan for: subscriber pseudonyms are personal data; user-count state size at fine grain; ingest batch sizes; a quota per consumer.
